questions.q: State the precise mathematical definition of an onto (surjective) function \( f: X \to Y \). Use quantifiers.
questions.a: Correct answer: \( \forall y \in Y, \; \exists x \in X \) such that \( f(x) = y \). A wrong answer like "every \( x \) has a unique \( y \)" confuses onto with the definition of a function; "distinct \( x \) give distinct \( y \)" describes one-one. This reveals the student does not distinguish between domain/codomain roles in surjectivity.

questions.q: Consider \( f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} \) defined by \( f(x) = x^2 \). A student claims: "Since every real number \( y \) has a square root, \( f \) is onto." Identify the flaw in this reasoning.
questions.a: The flaw: \( y = -1 \in \mathbb{R} \) has no real \( x \) with \( x^2 = -1 \). The student incorrectly assumed every real number has a real square root, ignoring that the square root of a negative number is not real. This reveals the misconception that "solving \( f(x)=y \) algebraically" is sufficient without checking if the solution lies in the specified domain.

questions.q: Determine whether \( f: \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z} \) defined by \( f(x) = 3x + 2 \) is onto. Show your work.
questions.a: Let \( y \in \mathbb{Z} \). Solve \( 3x + 2 = y \Rightarrow x = \frac{y-2}{3} \). For \( y = 0 \), \( x = -\frac{2}{3} \notin \mathbb{Z} \). Hence no integer \( x \) maps to 0. Therefore \( f \) is NOT onto. A wrong answer claiming it is onto typically forgets to verify that \( x \) is an integer; they only solve algebraically in \( \mathbb{R} \).

questions.q: Compare the functions \( f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}, f(x)=2x \) and \( g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}, g(x)=2x \). One is onto, the other is not. Which is which? Explain the role of the domain/codomain.
questions.a: \( g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} \) is onto because for any \( y \in \mathbb{R} \), \( x = y/2 \in \mathbb{R} \). \( f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \) is NOT onto because \( y=1 \in \mathbb{N} \) gives \( x=0.5 \notin \mathbb{N} \). The error is thinking the formula alone determines surjectivity; the sets \( X \) and \( Y \) are equally critical.

questions.q: A student proves \( f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}, f(x)=x^3 \) is onto by saying: "For any \( y \), take \( x = \sqrt[3]{y} \). Then \( f(x) = (\sqrt[3]{y})^3 = y \)." Is this proof complete? If not, what is missing?
questions.a: The proof is incomplete because it does not explicitly verify that \( \sqrt[3]{y} \in \mathbb{R} \) for every \( y \in \mathbb{R} \). While true, a rigorous proof must state: "Since the cube root of any real number is real, \( x \in \mathbb{R} \)." Missing this step shows the student does not understand that the pre-image must belong to the specified domain.

questions.q: Construct a function \( f: \{1,2,3\} \to \{a,b\} \) that is onto but not one-one. Draw its arrow diagram and explain why it satisfies surjectivity but fails injectivity.
questions.a: Example: \( f(1)=a, f(2)=b, f(3)=a \). Arrow diagram: 1→a, 2→b, 3→a. Every element of \( \{a,b\} \) has a pre-image (a has 1 and 3; b has 2), so onto. But \( f(1)=f(3)=a \) with \( 1 \neq 3 \), so not one-one. A poor answer might give a non-function or a function that misses an element of the codomain, showing confusion between the two properties.
